newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU and Mexico pave way for trade agreement.
newsitem.headline: EU and Mexico pave way for trade agreement.

text.p: The European Commission and Mexico have agreed an interim accord that paves the way for negotiations to begin early next year on a full free-trade pact, officials said on Thursday.

"I am very pleased to say that we have reached the point where we now have an interim agreement," said Jaime Zabludovsky, Mexico's deputy trade minister. "This needs to be approved by the European parliament and EU member states, but should be done later this year."
The Commission and Mexico have been haggling for years over the scope of a trade agreement -- particularly over European insistence that any deal should contain human rights clauses.

Mexico's ambassador to the European Union, Manuel Armandariz, said he was confident the interim agreement would satisfy both the European Parliament -- which insists on the human rights clause -- and conservative domestic politicians upset by what they see as interference in their affairs.

He said the political aspects of the agreement would allow for contacts between Mexico and the European Union "at the highest level" and also provide the opportunity for participation of non-governmental organisations in certain areas.
Trade between the EU and Mexico has dwindled over the past few years mainly because of the Latin American country's membership of the North American Free Trade Area (NAFTA).

European exporters have found it difficult to compete against NAFTA members who are able to sell goods to Mexico without punitive taxes and tariffs attached, while Mexican exports have also struggled against competition from countries which already have formal trade deals with the EU.

But with Mexico now claiming to be the world's 10th-biggest trader, EU companies are keen on a bigger slice of its $185 billion-a-year market than last year's 6.1 percent. In 1990, bilateral trade was nearly 11.5 percent of Mexican trade.
"The past few years have seen the EU having a smaller piece of a bigger pie," said Zabludovsky. "We certainly expect that the agreement will change this situation."

Asked if Mexico would be prepared to offer similar concessions to EU countries that it currently offers other NAFTA members, Zabludovsky said: "It is difficult to tell at this stage if the agreement will be identical (to NAFTA)."
"But I must stress that we are willing to put all kinds of disciplines on the agenda as long as they are consistent with domestic legislation."
Zabludovsky said that while a lot of work still had to be done in finalising a full free-trade agreement, the temporary accord would send a positive signal to financial markets.

"What happened in the case of the United States and Canada (during the NAFTA negotiations) was that once we had a clear set of objectives the signal transmitted to the economic actors was very, very important," he said.
"I think this will be the case with the European Union and Mexico.
